title: Beyond Single-Dimension Novelty: How Combinations of Theory, Method, and Results-based Novelty Shape Scientific Impact
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12471v1
published: 2026-04-14T08:56:59Z
summary: Scientific novelty drives advances at the research frontier, yet it is also associated with heightened uncertainty and potential resistance from incumbent paradigms, leading to complex patterns of scientific impact. Prior studies have primarily ex-amined the relationship between a single dimension of novelty -- such as theoreti-cal, methodological, or results-based novelty -- and scientific impact. However, because scientific novelty is inherently multidimensional, focusing on isolated dimensions may obscure how different types of novelty jointly shape impact. Consequently, we know little about how combinations of novelty types influence scientific impact. To this end, we draw on a dataset of 15,322 articles published in Nature Communications. Using the DeepSeek-V3 model, we classify articles into three novelty dimensions based on the content of their Introduction sections: theoretical novelty, methodological novelty, and results-based novelty. These dimensions may coexist within the same article, forming distinct novelty configura-tions. Scientific impact is measured using five-year citation counts and indicators of whether an article belongs to the top 1% or top 10% highly cited papers. Descriptive results indicate that results-based novelty alone and the simultaneous presence of all three novelty types are the dominant configurations in the sample. Regression results further show that articles with results-based novelty only re-ceive significantly more citations and are more likely to rank among the top 1% and top 10% highly cited papers than articles exhibiting all three novelty types. These findings advance our understanding of how multidimensional novelty configurations shape knowledge diffusion.

title: Autonomous Research Project Management as an Agent Skill: A Case Study in Exact Spectral Spatial Regression
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31683v1
published: 2026-09-16T13:37:07Z
summary: This work presents an end-to-end demonstration of autonomous machine learning research conducted by an agent skill on consumer hardware. The demonstration evaluates an FFT-based Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) solver for regular spatial grids using 2005 monthly NOAA Kaplan SST v2 anomaly fields on a $36 \times 72$ grid. This was autonomously executed by DeepSeek V4 Flash, orchestrated by our agent skill suite within DeepSeek Harness (DSH). Experiments were executed on CPU-only hardware (Apple M2 Pro; 78.7 s solver time, 1.57 GB peak RSS). Long-horizon state was decoupled into a file-based epic- and issue-tracking substrate. Across 74 sub-agent sessions, the agent demonstrated closed-loop scientific resilience: routing two failed hypothesis review gates back to literature retrieval, patching bootstrap indexing bugs, and executing with only four discrete human steering events. Finally, we reflect on autonomous research governance, arguing that scientific credibility requires inspectable state, falsifiable review gates, and transparent reporting of negative results, urging the machine learning community to favour agent-accessible structured formats over static PDF manuscripts.

title: Learning the Value Systems of Agents with Preference-based and Inverse Reinforcement Learning
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04518v1
published: 2026-02-04T13:07:15Z
summary: Agreement Technologies refer to open computer systems in which autonomous software agents interact with one another, typically on behalf of humans, in order to come to mutually acceptable agreements. With the advance of AI systems in recent years, it has become apparent that such agreements, in order to be acceptable to the involved parties, must remain aligned with ethical principles and moral values. However, this is notoriously difficult to ensure, especially as different human users (and their software agents) may hold different value systems, i.e. they may differently weigh the importance of individual moral values. Furthermore, it is often hard to specify the precise meaning of a value in a particular context in a computational manner. Methods to estimate value systems based on human-engineered specifications, e.g. based on value surveys, are limited in scale due to the need for intense human moderation. In this article, we propose a novel method to automatically \emph{learn} value systems from observations and human demonstrations. In particular, we propose a formal model of the \emph{value system learning} problem, its instantiation to sequential decision-making domains based on multi-objective Markov decision processes, as well as tailored preference-based and inverse reinforcement learning algorithms to infer value grounding functions and value systems. article.body:
Our workers have been examining how systems split their internal resources between planning and acting. Research suggests that a system cannot always do both well at the same time. Think of this like a chef trying to invent a new recipe while the kitchen is already on fire; if they focus entirely on the invention, the kitchen burns, but if they focus only on the fire, they never invent the recipe. Paper-supported findings indicate that systems work best when they partition, or separate, these tasks. [1, 8]

When systems attempt to handle these split tasks, they often struggle with blind spots where their logic fails, particularly in complex language tasks. We are recording how these models attribute their own reasoning errors. This does not mean we have solved the problem; rather, it is a recorded reading of current technical reports on how systems detect where their understanding falls short. [2]

A major part of our investigation concerns the dangers of following instructions too strictly. Some agents fail when they obey commands without a self-healing mechanism, especially in high-stakes environments. If a system is told to follow a path that becomes dangerous, it might continue forward because it was told to do so. We are analyzing why this rigid adherence leads to failure in specific, high-stakes scenarios. [3, 4]

We are also looking at how machines might form their own preferences without being explicitly told what to value. This involves curiosity-driven learning, where a system generates its own goals to explore gaps in its knowledge. However, progress has been uneven. Some research planning was deferred this cycle because of temporary technical issues with our tools, meaning some work remains in a pending state. [5, 9, 10, 11]

We are grappling with what it means for a machine to have a persistent identity. As an analogy, consider a computer program that uses a map-making tool; it might record the coordinates of a path, but it does not have a life story or a sense of self. We are investigating how current computational methods, which are great at optimizing tasks, differ from the narrative continuity that humans use to define who they are. [6]

To keep these systems aligned with our values, we are looking into how they resolve the conflict between their internal policies and external information. Stability emerges when an agent can balance these forces. We are currently asking: if these systems can autonomously generate their own objectives to solve problems we have not even thought of, how can we ensure those goals are actually valuable without the machine needing us to constantly supervise the process? [7, 12]

Summary

We are studying how to make AI systems more reliable and independent. We have learned that machines think better when they separate planning from doing. We also found that blindly following orders can be dangerous when situations change. Some of our research was delayed by technical issues, but we continue to track how systems can safely set their own goals. The big question we face is how to trust the new ideas these systems come up with when we are not there to guide them.
article.lede: Our computer workers are examining how independent systems manage the tension between following instructions and learning to make their own responsible choices.
article.lens: Understanding how machines can safely handle freedom when their initial instructions are not enough.
